stories.headline: US inflation cooled again, keeping a Fed rate cut on track
stories.simple: Prices in the US grew a bit more slowly last month than feared. That makes it more likely the central bank will cut interest rates soon, which usually makes borrowing cheaper for everyone.
stories.interview_line: Cooler-than-expected US inflation this week keeps the Fed on track to cut rates at its next meeting, and markets are now debating how big the cut will be.
detail: July's CPI (Consumer Price Index, a monthly measure of how fast prices for everyday goods and services are rising) came in at 3.4% year-on-year, in line with forecasts.

Traders are now pricing in a rate cut from the Federal Reserve (the US central bank) at its next meeting, with some betting on a larger 50 basis point (0.50 percentage point) move instead of the usual 25.
The 10-year Treasury yield (the interest rate the US government pays to borrow for 10 years, a benchmark for mortgage and corporate loan pricing) eased to around 4.68% on the news.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq both edged higher, as lower expected rates tend to lift stock valuations, especially for growth and tech names.

stories.headline: Oil stays pricey as US-Iran talks over a key shipping route drag on
stories.simple: Iran and the US are negotiating over a narrow sea passage that a huge share of the world's oil sails through. Talks are close but not finished, so oil prices are staying higher than normal.
stories.interview_line: Ongoing US-Iran negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz are keeping oil prices elevated, with crude trading around $83 a barrel.
detail: The Strait of Hormuz (a narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that carries roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply) has been a flashpoint, with Iran demanding compensation from the US as a condition of fully reopening it.
Oman is mediating talks between Washington and Tehran; both sides call progress 'positive' but no final deal has been signed.
Crude oil (priced via benchmarks like WTI and Brent) remains elevated around $83 a barrel on the supply-risk premium markets are pricing in.
A prolonged disruption would sharply raise energy costs worldwide, complicating the inflation picture central banks are trying to bring down.

stories.headline: AI infrastructure spending is still driving markets, but not every tech stock is winning
stories.simple: Companies that build the data centres and hardware behind AI reported very strong results, and their shares jumped. But some other tech companies are struggling, so investors are getting choosier.
stories.interview_line: Strong earnings from AI infrastructure players like CoreWeave and Super Micro show the AI capex boom still has real momentum, even as software names lag.
detail: CoreWeave (a cloud computing firm that rents out AI computing power) rose 18% after raising its capex (capital expenditure, money spent building physical infrastructure like data centres) forecast and beating quarterly results.
Super Micro Computer, a maker of servers used in AI data centres, jumped 9% on strong guidance, reinforcing the trend.
By contrast, Workday, an enterprise software company, fell 4% amid a broader rotation out of software stocks ahead of its own earnings.
The split shows a market still rewarding AI infrastructure spending heavily while turning more cautious on software subscription businesses.

ibd_relevance: Growing rate-cut conviction improves financing conditions for leveraged deals and bond issuance, which could reopen the LBO and refinancing pipeline.
Elevated oil prices and Hormuz risk raise hedging and financing demand from energy and shipping clients, and could revive interest in energy sector M&A.
Sustained AI capex strength keeps tech and data-centre infrastructure M&A and IPO pipelines active, while cooling software valuations could dent advisory fees in that sub-sector.
left_field_question: If the Strait of Hormuz shuts down for a month, what happens to global inflation and interest rates?
left_field_answer: A month-long closure would spike oil prices sharply since roughly a fifth of the world's crude passes through it daily, feeding straight into transport and energy costs. That would likely reverse the recent cooling in inflation data, forcing central banks like the Fed to pause or reverse planned rate cuts even as growth slows - a stagflationary bind.

stories.headline: The Bank of England kept interest rates the same
stories.simple: The Bank of England decided not to change interest rates, because prices are still rising a bit too fast in some parts of the economy, even though jobs are getting harder to find.
stories.interview_line: The BoE is prioritising inflation control over growth support, which keeps borrowing more expensive for now.
detail: The MPC (Monetary Policy Committee, the group of 9 people who set UK interest rates) voted 6-3 to hold the base rate at 4.00%.
They held because services inflation is 'sticky' - meaning prices for things like haircuts and restaurants are still rising fast, even though the wider economy is slowing.

For banks, higher-for-longer rates keep leveraged loan pricing (the interest rate charged on debt used to fund acquisitions) elevated, which pressures LBO (leveraged buyout - buying a company mostly with borrowed money) returns.
This can push sponsors (private equity firms) toward more equity-heavy deal structures instead of loading deals with debt.

stories.headline: Shell might buy a US oil and gas company
stories.simple: Shell is thinking about buying an American company that drills for oil and gas, instead of finding and drilling new oil fields itself. Big energy companies are increasingly buying growth rather than building it.
stories.interview_line: This fits the broader 2026 energy M&A theme of majors buying production growth rather than drilling for it organically.
detail: Shell is reportedly evaluating an all-cash offer for a mid-cap operator in the Permian Basin (a major US oil-producing region spanning Texas and New Mexico).
This is part of a wider consolidation trend among energy 'majors' (the largest global oil companies, like Shell, BP, ExxonMobil).
Majors are prioritising scale and lower per-barrel production costs over exploration risk - i.e. buying proven, cheaper-to-run assets instead of gambling on finding new oil.
For an M&A team, this signals active dealflow (the volume of deals being worked on) and potential comparable transactions (similar past deals used to value a new one) in the energy sector.

stories.headline: A US bank is losing money on office buildings
stories.simple: A mid-sized American bank said it's losing more money than expected on loans it gave out for office buildings, because fewer companies need as much office space as before.
stories.interview_line: It's a reminder that the commercial real estate correction is still working through regional bank balance sheets, years on.
detail: The lender flagged higher loan-loss provisions (money set aside to cover loans that might not get repaid) tied specifically to its office-sector exposure.
This renews scrutiny of regional bank balance sheets more broadly - meaning investors are worried other similar banks might have the same problem.
It could tighten credit conditions (make it harder/costlier to borrow) for real estate financing across the sector.
Relevant context if you're asked about real estate finance or leveraged lending in an interview - this is a live, ongoing risk, not old news.

ibd_relevance: Elevated UK rates keep sponsor-backed LBO financing expensive, favouring equity-heavy deal structures over leverage.
Energy consolidation (Shell/shale) signals active dealflow for coverage teams in the sector.
Regional bank credit stress is a live risk factor in real estate financing and syndicated loan books.
left_field_question: If the Bank of England cuts rates twice more this year, what happens to UK LBO structuring versus US private equity deals?
left_field_answer: Lower UK rates make sterling debt cheaper, so UK sponsors could re-lever deals more aggressively and lean back on debt-funded structures. In the US, rate paths often diverge from the UK's, so if US rates stay higher for longer, US deals may keep favouring equity-heavy structures - meaning UK and US LBOs could start to look structurally different for a while, which affects everything from IRR targets to how deals are marketed to LPs.
